pages.name: Steps For Teaching Phonics — Step 1
pages.subtitle: STEP 1 — SHORT VOWELS & CONSONANTS
pages.html:
Steps For Teaching Phonics
Step 1. Introduce the five short-vowel sounds together with the consonant sounds. Practise until they are secure.

Begin the first week with short-vowel flash cards. Each day add a few more consonant sounds so that, by the end of the week, the learner is reviewing every short vowel and every consonant. Do not hurry. Most children need two to four weeks of daily practice before these sounds become automatic.

Practical tip: Fifteen minutes of focused phonics work, five days a week, produces better results than longer, less frequent sessions.

pages.name: Steps 2 & 3 — Two & Three Letter Blends
pages.subtitle: TWO-LETTER & THREE-LETTER BLENDS
pages.html:
Step 2 & Step 3
Step 2. Practise joining two sounds. Keep going until blending feels effortless.

Once short vowels and consonants are known, teach the learner to slide two sounds together orally (b-a → ba) and then to read simple two-letter combinations such as ba, be, bi, bo, bu.

Two-Letter Blends
b + a = bas + a = sai + a = ia
b + e = bes + e = sei + e = ie
b + i = bis + i = sii + i = ii
b + o = bos + o = soi + o = io
b + u = bus + u = sui + u = iu
Step 3. Move on to three-letter blends (real words). Practise until reading is automatic.

When two-letter blends are easy, introduce three-letter words. Each day the learner should read a short list of short-vowel words and then write the same words from dictation.

Core principle: Never allow guessing, skipping or substituting. Accurate decoding always comes before speed.
Three-Letter Blends
fa + t = fatki + t = kitro + d = rod
de + n = denma + d = madse + t = set
bo + x = boxve + s = vestu + g = tug
hi + d = hidno + t = notwi + n = win

pages.name: Step 6 — High-Frequency Words
pages.subtitle: HIGH-FREQUENCY WORDS
pages.html:
Step 6. Introduce a small set of high-frequency words needed for most sentences.

After the learner can read three- and four-letter words smoothly, add a few essential high-frequency words. Some of these words follow regular patterns (for example “or”); others contain letters that do not behave in the expected way (for example “once” and “who”).

Write each word on a card. Introduce three or four new words each week and review them daily, encouraging the learner to use as much sound knowledge as possible. Once a word is mastered, move the card to a “Words I Know” pile. When an irregular word appears later, make a new card and place it in a “Words To Learn” pile.

Why this list is different: Many of the words below cannot be fully sounded out with early phonics knowledge. Ordinary “sight-word” lists often force children to memorise words that could actually be decoded once the right patterns have been taught.

Step 12. After three to four months of daily instruction, begin short decodable stories.

All the sounds and spellings listed in Steps 1–11 should be introduced within the first four months.

Step 13. Move gradually into easy-to-read books.

Continue systematic lessons even after the learner can read simple books. Most children need one to two years of reinforcement before the knowledge becomes permanent.

Step 14. Keep providing phonetically organised spelling lists.

Even after the formal programme ends, weekly spelling lists based on the patterns already taught help lock the knowledge in place.

pages.name: Introduction
pages.subtitle: HOW TO USE THIS BOOK
pages.html:
Introduction

Reading begins early. Children need daily contact with letters, words, sentences and stories. They also need clear, systematic teaching of how the written code works.

This book supplies practical guidance and carefully sequenced practice. The phonics steps that appear in the front matter follow a well-established order used by successful literacy programmes. They help teachers and parents know exactly what to teach and when.

Many adults worry about the best way to start. The process does not have to be complicated. Consistent short sessions that focus on one pattern at a time produce steady progress.

Ten to fifteen minutes of focused work most days is enough for most learners to move forward with confidence. Once a child can decode, he or she can begin to read for information and pleasure across every subject.

The vocabulary activities in each unit also expand the words a child can use in speech and in writing.

Crystal Phonics • Grade 5 PhonicsFront MatterPage 13

pages.name: Synthetic Phonics Instructions
pages.subtitle: NOTES
pages.html:
Synthetic Phonics Instructions

Before a child can read, the letters of the alphabet and the sounds they represent must be known. The letter A, for example, is linked to the short /a/ sound. Successful reading requires rapid recognition of both the letter shape and its sound.

This approach is called synthetic (or inductive) phonics: the learner builds words by putting individual sounds together.

Always present the letter name and the letter sound at the same time. Teaching them separately has little value. Research shows that children learn letter–sound links most readily when the name of the letter itself gives a clue to the sound.

Crystal Phonics • Grade 5 PhonicsFront MatterPage 14

pages.name: Developing Phonemic Awareness
pages.subtitle: NOTES
pages.html:
Developing Phonemic Awareness

Most people have heard of phonics, yet fewer understand phonemic awareness. It is one of the strongest predictors of later reading success.

Phonemic awareness is the ability to notice, identify and work with the individual sounds (phonemes) inside spoken words. In the word “cat”, the three phonemes are /c/, /a/ and /t/.

Children who can hear and manipulate these small units of sound usually make faster progress in both reading and spelling.

Blending Practice

Begin with simple oral stretching. For example, when you want a child to call someone, you might say the name slowly and stretched: “Call your mmmmaaammmaa.” The child hears the sounds being blended together.

b-a → ba → bbbbbaaaaa
s-a → sa → sssssaaaaaa
j-a → ja → jjjjjjjjjjjjaaaaa

pages.name: Consonant and Vowel Blends
pages.subtitle: NOTES
pages.html:
Consonant and Vowel Blends

So how do you help a young child develop phonemic awareness? One of the best ways is through blending. We'll touch on that in this book as we move on.

Learning to read at a young age is important for the development of the child. It helps them develop a better understanding of their surroundings, allows them to gather information from printed materials, and provides them with a wonderful source of entertainment when they read stories and rhymes.

Teach consonant and vowel blends first. Teaching words such "ba" and "be" can lead your child directly to learning words that rhyme with these. For example, for "ba", you can have: bad, band, bark, bath, back, etc.

You can start teaching blends once your child has learned the sounds of some consonants and short vowel sounds. You don't need to wait until your child has mastered the sounds of all the letters before teaching blends.

The lessons in our books start teaching your child blends almost right away, using the letter knowledge that they've learned. Our books are a truly logical and sequential method of teaching your child to read, that produces fantastic results.

One of the best ways to help your child develop phonemic awareness is through practicing "blending".

Crystal Phonics • Grade 5 PhonicsFront MatterPage 16

pages.name: Blending Practice
pages.subtitle: NOTES
pages.html:
Blending Practice

Being able to blend and segment words helps children to read and spell. According to the National Reading Panel, blending helps children develop reading skills where printed letters are turned into sounds which combine to form words.

Start blending practice with some ear training with your child. For example, if you wanted to ask your child to call his mother, you could say: "Aseda, call your mmmmaaammmaa." The word mama is sounded out slow and "stretchy". The level of sound separation can be set by you to increase or lower the difficulty.

Below are some sample words which you can use to play blending sounds activities with your child.

b-a ba bbbbbaaaaa
s-a sa sssssaaaaaa
j-a ja jjjjjjjjjjjjaaaaa

Our phonics book is designed to help you easily teach your child to develop exceptional reading skills. It will allow you to help your child develop phonemic awareness and reading fluency through the step-by-step lessons contained in our books. Simple, effective, and the results you will see are real. Simply follow the steps given in this book and your child will become a thriving reader.

Crystal Phonics • Grade 5 PhonicsFront MatterPage 17

pages.name: Teacher / Parent Methodology
pages.subtitle: ORAL AND AUDIOVISUAL TRAINING
pages.html:
Methodology
Oral and Audiovisual Training (Sight and Ear Training)

Using the oral and audiovisual training steps:

  • LOOK at the letters.
  • STUDY the letters with their names "A" and sounds /a/.
  • SAY the names "A" and the sounds /a/ aloud for the child to be able to recognize the names "a" and the sounds /a/ on the next page.
Note: Young children have short attention spans, and this is even more so for very young children such as a two or three year old. Therefore, your aim should be to engage them often in short and brief "learning" sessions throughout the day. Each session should last just 2 to 5 minutes. For older children depending on their age and level of maturity, you can lengthen the sessions to 10 to 15 minutes. But always remember that this should never seem like a chore that turns the child off from reading.
Crystal Phonics • Grade 5 PhonicsFront MatterPage 18

pages.name: Daily Session Guidance
pages.subtitle: NOTES
pages.html:
Daily Session Guidance

Typically, 10 to 15 minutes per day total spread across several sessions is more than sufficient to teach your child to read.

You may be thinking "can I really teach my child to read with just 15 minutes a day?" YES YOU CAN. The key is consistency and patience, and not trying to teach 30 minutes one day, and then doing nothing for another three days.

pages.html:
Pronunciation Sounds and Spelling

There are 26 letters in the English alphabet but there are 44 sounds in the English language. This means that the number of sounds in a word is not always the same as the number of letters.

The word "CAT" has three letters and three sounds but the word "CATCH" has five letters but still only three sounds.

If we write these words using phonemic sounds, we can see exactly how many sounds they have.

CAT = /k/ /a/ /t/
CATCH = /k/ /a/ /tch/

In "CATCH" the three letters TCH are one sound.
